attestations.notes: Read Proof 1.1–4.1: nonempty logical domain supplies one set, Separation with z≠z gives existence, and Extensionality gives uniqueness; no set-theoretic empty-set axiom or choice is assumed.

Read Proof 1.1–4.1: x≠∅ supplies a single member B; Separation within B gives the full intersection and Extensionality removes dependence on B. The nonempty-family restriction is essential and retained.
Read Proof 1.1–4.1: the containing set supplied by Power Set is restricted by Separation to exactly the subsets of x; Extensionality gives uniqueness, including x=∅.
Read Proof 1.1–2.1: checked all five membership equivalences, including empty union and nonempty singleton/pair intersections. No empty-family intersection is asserted.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: both {a} and {a,b} lie in P(A∪B), so their Kuratowski pair lies in P(P(A∪B)). Empty A or B has no witness and is vacuous.
Read Proof 1.1–4.1: checked both directions and the a=b/a≠b split; reverse memberships exclude a collapsed target pair in the distinct case. Singleton specialization is valid.
Read Proof 1.1–4.1: checked both unordered-pair alternatives for Kuratowski equality; the swapped alternative forces all entries equal, so both coordinates agree. Converse is substitution.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: Kuratowski coordinates lie in the double union of R; Separation with R as parameter forms both domain and range. Empty R produces empty sets.

Read Proof 1.1–3.1: Separation inside one Infinity witness defines the intersection of all inductive sets without forming a class-sized intersection; successor closure and mutual inclusion establish minimality and uniqueness.
Read Proof 1.1–5.1: the inductive subset contains ω by minimality; Separation gives the property version and membership gives the converse.

Read Proof 1.1–3.1: simultaneous induction proves transitivity and self-nonmembership; both successor self-membership alternatives contradict the inductive hypothesis, without appealing to Foundation.

Read Proof 1.1–6.1: nonempty closed-subset intersection supplies the least relation; deleting an extraneous value at zero or a successor preserves closure using P1/P2. Induction gives total single-valuedness and uniqueness; a∈A excludes an empty codomain.
Read Proof 1.1–2.1: induction supplies P3, successor contains its predecessor for P1, and transitivity plus self-nonmembership rule out mutually incident unequal predecessors for P2.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: recursion with A=ℕ and f=σ gives a unique total s_m for every m, hence total addition and both recursion equations, including m=0.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: induction on c, with a,b fixed, uses only the addition recursion and its induction hypothesis; both base sides reduce to a+b.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: induction on n proves the left zero identity from the right-recursive addition clauses; the right identity remains definitional.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: induction on the second summand establishes the left successor law without assuming commutativity.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: the n=0 case uses the left zero identity; the successor case uses the independently proved left successor law and the right-recursive definition.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: induction quantifies over both m,n at each k; successor injectivity reduces the successor cancellation case to its hypothesis.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: the subset of zero and successor numbers contains zero and every σ(n), so induction proves exhaustion; the nonzero hypothesis selects the successor branch.

Read Proof 1.1–3.1: addition cancellation excludes positive increment fixed points and opposite strict inequalities; induction on n treats m<n, m=n and m>n with the successor decomposition of the nonzero difference.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: checked reflexivity, witness addition for transitivity, zero-sum exclusion by the successor axiom, cancellation for antisymmetry and trichotomy for totality.
Read Proof 1.1–2.1: successor decomposition proves the forward order implication; backward uses cancellation and σ(i)≠0. The already established linear order excludes a point between n and σ(n).
Read Proof 1.1–2.1: each relation element has coordinates in its domain/range; coordinate uniqueness supplies the reverse inclusion test, including the empty relation.
Read Proof 1.1–2.1: inverse and composition are separated inside their indicated products, restriction inside R; existential middle-coordinate witnesses require no choice.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: successor has no fixed point by induction, using P1 at zero and P2 in the successor case.

Read Proof 1.1–6.1: proved ω transitive first, then both membership/order implications by induction. Mixed order transitivity and discreteness precede their uses; subset equivalence uses self-nonmembership, avoiding ordinal circularity.

Read Proof 1.1–7.1: codomain transposition normalizes the top value and restriction contradicts the induction hypothesis. Checked zero case and all four consequences, including a missing point in a proper subset and both trichotomy directions; only individual witnesses are selected.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: under absence of a minimum the initial avoidance set contains zero and is successor closed, using the derived m<σ(n)⇒m≤n; induction contradicts nonemptiness.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: recursion with initial zero and add_m supplies a unique total multiplication sequence for every m, including m=0.
Read Proof 1.1–2.1: reorder the additive witness for both weak-order directions and cancel in the reverse direction; cancellation also preserves/reflexively reflects inequality for the strict forms.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: right unit follows at σ(0); simultaneous induction establishes left zero and left unit using n+1=σ(n).

Read Proof 1.1–3.1: separate inductions establish left distributivity and the left successor law; only addition associativity/commutativity and the recursion are used, before multiplication commutativity.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: induction on n uses independently established left zero and left successor laws; no multiplicative commutativity is presumed in its inputs.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: induction on c uses the multiplication recursion and previously proved left distributivity; zero case and closure are valid.
Read Proof 1.1–4.1: contrapositive writes each nonzero factor as a successor, making the product a successor via the two recursion equations; P1 excludes zero.
Read Proof 1.1–2.1: right distributivity transports the additive gap; strictness requires k≠0 and uses absence of natural zero divisors plus additive cancellation. k=0 only gives the weak inequality.
Read Proof 1.1–4.1: checked quotient cross-sum equations for addition and swapped-coordinate negation, using natural associativity/commutativity.
Read Proof 1.1–5.1: factor the cross-sums through the common value a+b′=b+a′; symmetry handles the second representative, then both replacements compose.
Read Proof 1.1–2.1: checked representative expansions for addition, inverses, multiplication associativity, identity and distributivity; quotient operation independence is supplied first.

Read Proof 1.1–5.1: cross-sum order is representative independent by translated cancellation; transitivity uses a common natural offset. Positive products have the nonzero natural gap km; reflexivity is immediate from the defining comparison.
Read Proof 1.1–4.1: distributivity gives 0a=0a+0a; additive cancellation gives 0a=0 in any field. Commutativity permits the stated cancellation orientation.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: difference identities and positive-cone addition prove translation invariance and addition of strict inequalities for arbitrary field elements.
Read Proof 1.1–4.1: distributivity and zero multiplication identify each negative product as an additive inverse; uniqueness and double negation give (-a)(-b)=ab.

Read Proof 1.1–4.1: checked all sign products and both directions of the positive/negative multiplier equivalences. Trichotomy excludes equality and the opposite inequality; zero multipliers are excluded by strict sign premises.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: nonzero trichotomy gives exactly two sign cases; positive-cone multiplicative closure and the two-negative product identity make each square positive.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: field nondegeneracy gives 1≠0; applying the nonzero-square result and 1²=1 proves 0<1.
Read Proof 1.1–5.1: a positive element has a nonzero inverse, whose negative sign would contradict 0<1. Multiplication by a⁻¹b⁻¹ reverses reciprocal order for 0<a<b.

Read Proof 1.1–2.1: group associativity and commutativity prove identity and inverse uniqueness in the additive group and the nonzero multiplicative group; inverse notation explicitly excludes zero in the conclusion.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: all nonzero integer sign patterns give nonzero products in the ordered ring; applying this to (x−y)z proves cancellation when z≠0.

Read Proof 1.1–4.1: evaluating e*f two ways identifies any left and right identity; all stated uniqueness consequences follow without associativity. Existence of the witnesses excludes an empty carrier.
Read Proof 1.1–3.1: checked product, sum and negation cross-multiplications under ab′=a′b and cd′=c′d. Integer no-zero-divisor property ensures the resulting denominator products are admissible.

Read Proof 1.1–2.1: checked all rational ring representative formulas, distributivity up to common nonzero scaling, 1≠0 and inversion of a nonzero numerator. Integer cancellation/no-zero-divisors protect denominators.

Read Proof 1.1–4.1: comparisons use positive denominators; positive integer scaling proves representative invariance, transitivity and additive compatibility. Positive numerators and denominator products give product positivity; reflexivity is immediate.

Read Proof 1.1–4.1: h*(g*h′)=(h*g)*h′ is the single associativity use; both inverse equations and the two-sided identity give h=h′. A lone one-sided equation identifies the inverse only when g is already invertible.

Read Proof 1.1–3.1: positivity and strict increments follow from 0<1; induction gives addition and multiplication compatibility of canonical naturals. All displayed strict-positivity claims restrict n≥1.

Read Proof 1.1–2.1: cross-sum equality proves injection; explicit pair arithmetic preserves both operations and the comparison preserves/reflexively reflects order. The nonnegative representative gap gives image surjectivity and uniqueness.
